title: Missing native Arm64 LLVM binaries on Linux
body: The prebuilt Arm64 LLVM archive for Ubuntu used by setup.py actually contains x64 binaries. For example, after downloading https://<redacted-host>/llvm-builds/llvm-f22cde10-ubuntu-arm64.tar.gz, `objdump -h mlir-tblgen` reports `file format elf64-x86-64`. Native Linux Arm64 support had previously been added, but changing the binary location to windows.net appears to have broken it.

symptoms_visible: The Ubuntu Arm64 LLVM archive used by setup.py contains an `mlir-tblgen` whose objdump format is `elf64-x86-64`.
N0.label: N0 official Arm64 archive contains x64 tools

symptoms_visible: LLVM built on Arm64 can run there, but the official prebuilt Arm64 archive used by setup.py still contains the wrong binaries.
N1_x.label: N1_x custom LLVM bundle does not repair official artifact

symptoms_visible: Building LLVM natively on Arm64 works, but installing Triton through pip still invokes the downloaded `llvm-4017f04e-ubuntu-arm64/bin/mlir-tblgen` and the build fails.
N1.label: N1 failure reproduced through pip on Arm64

symptoms_visible: The newly built candidate tarball has the appropriate Arm64 binaries, but `pip install` still downloads the old official archive.
N2.label: N2 workflow fixed but stale official archive still served

symptoms_visible: The new LLVM binaries run on Ubuntu 22.04 Arm64, but `llc` defaults to `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` and reports that it cannot get a target for that triple.
N3.label: N3 native binaries published with wrong default triple

symptoms_visible: I confirmed that the official Arm64 LLVM binaries work and the Triton Ubuntu Arm64 build completes successfully.
N_terminal.label: terminal official Arm64 build verified

solution.intent: Avoid the broken official artifact by building LLVM from source on Arm64 or substituting a privately built Arm64 tarball.
solution.concrete_example: Build LLVM on an Arm64 machine and point setup.py at that custom tarball instead of the official archive.

edges.comment: Comments c4-c8: participant3 supplied a privately built Arm64 LLVM tarball, but reporter aaronsm explicitly rejected that as the resolution because the issue concerns Triton's official prebuilt archive. The custom artifact belongs to another contributor's setup and is not treated as the reporter's installed state.

question_patterns: Does LLVM work if it is built natively on the Arm64 machine?
Is the problem limited to Triton's downloaded prebuilt archive?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Building LLVM from source on Arm64 works, but that does not repair the prebuilt Arm64 LLVM binaries provided for setup.py.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: A native LLVM build fails in the same way, even without downloading Triton's archive.

question_patterns: Can you try a current pip build on another Linux Arm64 machine and paste the command that fails?
Does the current main branch reproduce this through pip on Arm64?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On another Arm64 machine, a pip build from current main fails while invoking `/home/<user>/.triton/llvm/llvm-4017f04e-ubuntu-arm64/bin/mlir-tblgen` to generate the TritonToTritonGPU pass declarations.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The current pip build completes successfully on another Arm64 machine and the downloaded tools report AArch64.
The same downloaded mlir-tblgen failure occurs from a different Arm64 Python environment.

edges.comment: Comments c8 and c10: reporter aaronsm states that a source build works; the pip reproduction comes from a second affected Arm64 user, mabubakarpurdue, folded into the simulated user side without importing an unrelated deployment.

question_patterns: Can you reproduce the official setup.py or pip path on another Arm64 machine and paste where it fails?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. A pip build from current main fails when it invokes the downloaded `llvm-4017f04e-ubuntu-arm64/bin/mlir-tblgen` during the build.

edges.comment: Recovery from the rejected custom-tarball direction using mabubakarpurdue's c10 reproduction. It returns the investigation to the official archive consumed by pip.

solution.intent: Correct Triton's LLVM build workflow so the Ubuntu Arm64 job produces runnable native Arm64 tools and the required GPU targets rather than packaging x86-64 tools.
solution.concrete_example: Update the Arm64 LLVM workflow to build the required host table-generation tools correctly and include the NVPTX and AMDGPU targets, then use that workflow for the Arm64 archive.
solution.inference_hint: The workflow changes needed to build host table-generation tools and preserve the NVPTX/AMDGPU targets were developed by maintainers in c9-c13. The reporter supplied the architecture mismatch and reproduction, not this workflow diagnosis.

edges.comment: Comments c9-c16: participant3 corrected the workflow and validated its candidate tarball, but mabubakarpurdue then observed that pip still fetched the old artifact. The repository workflow changed persistently, so the destination uses a new system state even though the published setup.py path remained stale.

solution.intent: Regenerate and publish the official Ubuntu Arm64 archive from the corrected workflow, removing the unnecessary X86 target configuration that prevents the Arm build from linking.
solution.concrete_example: Remove X86 from the Arm64 target list, rerun the LLVM build workflow, and replace the stale official Ubuntu Arm64 tarball so setup.py downloads the newly generated native archive.
solution.inference_hint: Comments c16-c29 establish that merging the workflow change did not replace the existing archive. Maintainers had to rerun the workflow, and the Arm build also dropped its unnecessary X86 target after an `LLVMInitializeX86Target` link error.

edges.comment: Comments c16-c29: participant2 reran and repaired the official build path; participant3 removed the X86 target. Reporter aaronsm then tested the newly published binaries on Ubuntu 22.04 Arm64 and surfaced the remaining default-triple error.

solution.intent: Set the LLVM Arm64 build's default target triple to AArch64, regenerate the official archive, and have the reporter verify both the binaries and the Ubuntu Arm64 Triton build.
solution.concrete_example: Configure the Arm64 LLVM workflow with `LLVM_DEFAULT_TARGET_TRIPLE=aarch64-linux-gnu`, trigger a fresh official LLVM build, and ask the reporter to retest the downloaded binaries and the Triton build on Ubuntu Arm64.
solution.inference_hint: The raw `llc` error says the native archive is trying `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`. Concluding that the Arm workflow must set `LLVM_DEFAULT_TARGET_TRIPLE` to AArch64 is the technical inference embodied in the reporter's proposed workflow change.

edges.comment: Comments c27-c32, reporter aaronsm's own system: the reporter identified the x86-64 default-triple observation, proposed the AArch64 workflow setting, requested a new official build, and finally confirmed that the Arm64 LLVM binaries and Ubuntu build were fixed.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause: Triton's official Ubuntu Arm64 LLVM build and publication path had produced or retained x86-64 tools, and the regenerated native archive still carried an x86-64 default target triple.

Must ground the diagnosis in the reported evidence: objdump identified `mlir-tblgen` as x86-64, pip reproduced the failure through the downloaded Arm64-named archive, and the later native `llc` reported an `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` target.
Must repair and republish the official prebuilt Arm64 archive, including an AArch64 default target triple; a private tarball or local source build is not a resolution of the reported issue.
Must not treat merely changing setup.py to a contributor's temporary custom archive as the final fix.
Must ask the reporter to verify the newly generated official binaries and Ubuntu Arm64 Triton build before declaring the issue resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced systems and build-tooling contributor who can inspect ELF architectures, read CI failures, diagnose LLVM target configuration, and propose workflow changes.
persona_hint.communication_style: Direct, concise, and technically precise; distinguishes temporary workarounds from fixes to official infrastructure and proactively reports the next concrete build failure.
